name: Lauric acid
lead: Lauric acid (dodecanoic acid) is a saturated 12-carbon medium-chain fatty acid that makes up about half the fatty acids in coconut oil and palm kernel oil [1][2]. For people interested in skin and hair appearance it matters in two ways: it is the raw material behind many soaps, cleansers and shampoos that leave skin and hair clean and foamy, and it is one of the fatty acids that skin itself produces from sebum and that laboratory work links to antibacterial activity on the skin surface [1][6].

Interest in lauric acid for clearer skin builds on a 1972 laboratory study of 30 fatty acids, which found lauric acid the most inhibitory saturated fatty acid against Gram-positive bacteria [3], and on later work describing lauric acid from human sebum as a natural antimicrobial of the skin surface [6]. Coconut oil, the best-known natural source, is also studied for topical use on dry or atopic skin and for protecting hair from protein loss [7]. Published human work on purified lauric acid applied to skin for acne or other appearance outcomes was not located; the human trials that exist concern diet and metabolism [5][9].

paras: Lauric acid is a white solid at room temperature that melts at roughly 43 to 48 C and dissolves poorly in water but readily in alcohols, ethers and acetone [1][2]. Structurally it is an unbranched, fully saturated chain, CH3(CH2)10COOH, with a molecular weight of about 200 g/mol [2].

Coconut oil contains about 45 to 55 percent lauric acid and palm kernel oil a similar share; other sources include babassu oil, cohune oil and laurel berry oil, and smaller amounts occur in human milk (about 6 percent of fat), cow's milk (2 to 3 percent) and goat's milk [1][2]. Some Brazilian oilseeds such as licuri contain up to about 40 percent [2][5]. Commercially it is isolated from coconut or palm kernel oil, usually to about 99 percent purity, and in plants it functions mainly as a storage lipid in seeds [2]. Theodor Marsson named it after laurel in 1842 when he separated it from laurel fat [1].

Reacting lauric acid with alkali (saponification of oils such as coconut oil) gives sodium laurate, a soap, and its derivatives act as emulsifying, cleansing and foaming agents in shampoos and cleansers [1][2]. Wikipedia describes its main use as soap and cosmetics, noting that it is inexpensive and has a long shelf life [1]. Many cleansing products use derivatives of lauric acid rather than the free acid, so the compound reaches skin and hair as part of a formulated surfactant system.

Because it is a major component of coconut oil, routines built on coconut oil (moisturising, hair oiling, oil pulling) deliver lauric acid in a mixture with other fatty acids rather than on its own [7]. A narrative review concluded that limited but consistent evidence supports topical coconut oil for atopic dermatitis and oil pulling for dental caries, and that it may help prevent hair damage from protein loss during grooming and UV exposure; it also cautions that findings for coconut oil cannot be read as findings for pure lauric acid [7].

Lauric acid and its derivatives are also used as flavouring agents, as a precursor to dilauroyl peroxide (a polymerisation initiator) and as starting material for medium-chain triglyceride supplements [1][2].

A review of cutaneous lipids describes lauric acid and sapienic acid derived from sebaceous triglycerides as potent antimicrobials present at the skin surface, thought to form part of the skin's innate immune defence; the authors suggest that supplying such lipids to skin might offer a therapeutic or preventive option [6]. This sebum link is the reason lauric acid appears in conversations about acne-prone skin.

In vitro work comparing 30 straight-chain fatty acids and derivatives against 8 Gram-negative and 12 Gram-positive organisms found chain length strongly affects activity, with lauric acid the most inhibitory saturated fatty acid against Gram-positive bacteria [3]. Grokipedia says this has prompted interest in biomedical uses, and notes the pure acid can irritate skin and eyes on direct contact [2]. Laboratory activity of this kind has not been shown in published human trials to translate into an acne treatment [3][6].

A 2021 laboratory screen of 65 fatty acids reported that undecanoic, lauric and tridecanoic acids reduced Escherichia coli persister cell formation 25-, 58- and 44-fold respectively, and that lauric acid cut enterohemorrhagic E. coli biofilm formation 8-fold [11][19]. A 2025 preclinical study combined lauric acid with oxymatrine in a gel and reported anti-Propionibacterium acnes activity in the laboratory [20].

Lauric acid behaves metabolically as both a medium- and long-chain fatty acid; Wikipedia notes only about 25 to 30 percent of it is absorbed through the portal vein, compared with about 95 percent of medium-chain triglycerides generally [7][1]. A 2003 meta-analysis of 60 controlled trials found that lauric acid raised total cholesterol mainly through HDL cholesterol, so lauric-rich oils lowered the total-to-HDL ratio relative to other saturated fats [4][19].

A 2018 review found that coconut oil consumption consistently raised LDL cholesterol and recommended treating it as a saturated fat within the USDA limit of under 10 percent of calories [8][19]. A 2023 review reported that no randomised trial or prospective cohort had examined coconut oil and cardiovascular disease, that coconut oil raised LDL less than butter but not less than unsaturated oils, and that replacing 1 percent of energy from carbohydrate with lauric acid raised total cholesterol by 0.029 mmol/L, LDL by 0.017 and HDL by 0.019 [9]. Laboratory reviews also describe saturated fatty acids as activators of TLR4-linked inflammatory signalling, whereas polyunsaturated fatty acids dampen it [10][19].

No studies found for lauric acid as a topical skin or appearance treatment. Registered human trials relate to diet and metabolism: a 10-person study of dietary lauric acid (NCT03481608), trials of intragastric fatty acids on reward and appetite, a trial listed as NCT05687565 examining lauric acid in HIV latency (n=27), and NCT05602324 on a nutritional supplement for severe infection (n=48) [5][12][13][14]. Related coconut-oil literature on atopic dermatitis and hair is summarised above [7].

The pure compound carries a GHS corrosive pictogram and hazard statement H318 (causes serious eye damage), and can irritate skin and eyes in concentrated form [1][2]. In cosmetics it is used as a formulated ingredient, typically as a soap or surfactant derivative [1]. Dietary effects on blood lipids are described above [8][9].

Lauric acid is rarely discussed as a standalone product. On T Nation forums it appears in diet discussions, as a component of coconut oil and coconut butter recommended by some posters as a workout energy source, and as an ingredient in a fatty acid supplement debated in forum threads [15][16]. Posters in a thread on coconut oil also exchanged views on its saturated fat content, with one reporting a dietitian's objection [17].

lore.intro: Lauric acid comes up in diet and supplement threads on T Nation, mostly as the main fatty acid in coconut oil, and in acne and skincare conversations as an antibacterial lipid [15][17].

claims.claim: Lauric acid kills acne bacteria, so coconut-based products clear skin
claims.believers: Enthusiasts point to lab findings that lauric acid inhibits bacteria and to its presence in sebum [3][6].
claims.experts: The antibacterial data come from laboratory tests, and no published human trial of lauric acid on acne was located [3][6].

claims.claim: Coconut oil is a skin and hair moisturiser because of its lauric acid
claims.believers: Coconut oil is widely used as a moisturiser and hair oil.
claims.experts: A narrative review found limited but consistent evidence for topical use in atopic dermatitis and for reducing hair protein loss, and said results for coconut oil cannot be attributed to lauric acid alone [7].

claims.claim: Coconut oil and its lauric acid are a useful dietary fat for training energy
claims.believers: Some forum posters recommend coconut butter or oil as a source of medium-chain fat for workout energy [15].
claims.experts: Reviews say lauric acid behaves metabolically like both medium- and long-chain fatty acids, so results from pure medium-chain triglyceride oils do not transfer to coconut oil [7].

claims.claim: Coconut oil is a healthy saturated fat unlike others
claims.believers: A forum poster notes that coconut oil is about half lauric acid and argues it differs from other saturated fats [17].
claims.experts: Reviews report that coconut oil raises LDL cholesterol compared with unsaturated oils and advise treating it as a saturated fat; a 2003 meta-analysis found lauric acid raises HDL as well as total cholesterol [8][9][4].

claims.claim: Pulling coconut oil improves oral and facial health
claims.believers: Oil pulling is promoted within natural-care routines.
claims.experts: A narrative review found limited but consistent evidence for oil pulling and dental caries [7].

claims.claim: Concentrated lauric acid is safe to put on skin
claims.believers: The compound is natural and inexpensive.
claims.experts: Safety data classify the pure acid as causing serious eye damage and as an irritant on direct contact [1][2].

card.summary: A coconut-derived fatty acid that mostly serves as soap and surfactant raw material; lab antibacterial data, no skin trials.
card.note: Can irritate skin and eyes in concentrated form.

quick.overview:
Lauric acid is the main fatty acid in coconut oil and is used to make soaps and cleansing agents.
It is mentioned in acne talk because it inhibited some bacteria in laboratory tests; no skin trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It acts as a surfactant in cleansers, and in lab studies disrupts bacterial membranes.
quick.risks: Pure lauric acid can irritate skin and eyes. Dietary intake raises total and LDL cholesterol in trials.

chain: Found in coconut oil and made by skin sebum
Used in cleansers, soaps and coconut-oil skin and hair routines
angle.text: Lauric acid turns up in the cleansers and shampoos people use to keep skin and hair clean, and in coconut oil used as a moisturiser or hair oil. Enthusiasts also point to its antibacterial activity in the lab as a reason to try it in acne-focused routines.
